title: The Temple Sermon: A Den of Robbers
summary: God sends Jeremiah to stand at the temple gate and tell the worshipers that the temple will not save them. They chant that this is the temple of the LORD while they steal, murder, commit adultery, oppress the vulnerable, and worship Baal, as if the sanctuary were a robbers' hideout. God will do to this house what he did to Shiloh. He forbids Jeremiah to pray for them, condemns the worship of the Queen of Heaven and the burning of children at Topheth, and declares that obedience, not sacrifice, was his first command.
story: Chapters 2 to 6 announced judgment on Judah in poetry. Chapter 7 opens a new section (chapters 7 to 10) with prose, and it takes aim at the one thing Judah was sure could not fall: the temple in Jerusalem. The people remembered that God had delivered Jerusalem from the Assyrian king Sennacherib in 701 BC (Isaiah 37), and many drew the conclusion that God would never let his house be destroyed. Jeremiah says otherwise. The same sermon is told again as a story in chapter 26, where we learn that it nearly cost Jeremiah his life. The temple's fall, which he foretells here, will come in 587 or 586 BC and is narrated in chapter 52.
historical:
Chapter 26 dates the temple sermon to the beginning of the reign of Jehoiakim (26:1), about 609 or 608 BC. Josiah, the reforming king, had just been killed at Megiddo, and Egypt had placed his son Jehoiakim on the throne. The reforms Josiah had carried out quickly unraveled. Chapter 26 records that priests, prophets, and people seized Jeremiah and demanded his death for this sermon, and that some elders cited the prophet Micah, who had once foretold Jerusalem's ruin under Hezekiah (Micah 3:12), to argue for sparing him.

Shiloh, in the hill country of Ephraim, was where the tabernacle stood in the days of the judges and of Eli and Samuel (Joshua 18:1; 1 Samuel 1-4). The ark was captured by the Philistines in Eli's time, and Psalm 78:60-61 remembers God abandoning his dwelling at Shiloh; by Jeremiah's day it had long been a ruin. Topheth was a site in the Valley of Hinnom, just south and west of Jerusalem, where children were burned as offerings. Kings Ahaz and Manasseh are said to have made their sons pass through the fire (2 Kings 16:3; 21:6), and Josiah defiled Topheth to stop the practice (2 Kings 23:10), but it seems to have returned.
cultural:
The temple gate was the place where crowds entered for festivals and sacrifices, making it the most public pulpit in Judah. Worshipers often recited liturgies at the gate (compare Psalms 15 and 24, which ask who may enter God's house and answer with ethical requirements). Jeremiah's hearers apparently chanted a phrase of confidence instead, the temple of the LORD, three times over, as if the words themselves guaranteed safety.

The Queen of Heaven (verse 18) was a goddess, most likely the Mesopotamian Ishtar or a related West Semitic goddess such as Astarte, associated with the evening star, fertility, and war. Her worship was a family affair: children gathered wood, fathers lit fires, and women baked cakes, perhaps shaped in her image or marked with a star (44:19 speaks of cakes made in her image). Chapter 44 shows the refugees in Egypt still defending her worship. Cutting off one's hair (verse 29) was a sign of mourning, and the silencing of the voices of bride and bridegroom (verse 34) meant the end of weddings, the end of normal life and of the future.
literary: The chapter is prose sermon, in a style close to Deuteronomy, full of if-then conditions and lists of commandments. Verse 9 lists sins that match the Ten Commandments: stealing, murder, adultery, false swearing, and other gods. The sermon moves in blocks: the call to amend (verses 3 to 7), the false trust exposed (verses 8 to 15), the ban on intercession (verses 16 to 20), sacrifice versus obedience (verses 21 to 28), and a lament over Topheth (verses 29 to 34). Repetition carries the argument: the house which bears My Name appears again and again, reminding the hearers that the temple belongs to God, not to them. The triple chant in verse 4 is mocked by its very repetition.

outline.t: At the temple gate: amend your ways
A den of robbers; remember Shiloh
Do not pray for them: the Queen of Heaven
Lament for Topheth, the Valley of Slaughter

doctrines.note: God's presence in the temple was a gift, not a guarantee. A holy God cannot be used as a shield for unholy lives, and a sanctuary filled with people who break his commands becomes a den of robbers in his sight.

Judah combined worship of the LORD with worship of Baal and the Queen of Heaven and with child sacrifice at Topheth. The chapter shows that idolatry often coexists with busy religion, and that it harms the worshipers themselves: is it not themselves they spite?

God's first demand at the exodus was obedience: I will be your God, and you will be My people. Sacrifice had its place, but it was never meant to replace justice for the foreigner, the fatherless, and the widow, or faithfulness to God alone.

words.note: Batach, to trust or feel secure. Verses 4, 8, and 14 use it for the people's confidence in deceptive words and in the house in which you trust. Trust itself is good; the problem is its object. Jeremiah contrasts trust in God with trust in anything else, including sacred places (compare 17:5-8).

Sheqer, a lie or deception, one of Jeremiah's favorite words. The deceptive words of verses 4 and 8 are the slogans of false security. In Jeremiah, sheqer describes false prophecy, false gods, and false trust; it names whatever claims to give life and cannot.

Mearah, a cave. The den of robbers in verse 11 is literally a cave of violent men, the kind of hideout in the Judean hills where bandits retreated after a raid. The picture is precise: the temple has become the place where criminals go to feel safe between crimes, not a place of repentance.

Palal, to pray or intercede. Verse 16 forbids Jeremiah to pray for the people, a prohibition repeated in 11:14 and 14:11. Prophets were intercessors, like Moses and Samuel, so this is a sign that the time for turning back the judgment has passed, though Jeremiah's grief for his people continues.

christ: When Jesus drove the money changers out of the temple, he quoted this chapter: My house will be called a house of prayer, but you have made it a den of robbers (Matthew 21:13; Mark 11:17, combining Isaiah 56:7 with Jeremiah 7:11). By choosing Jeremiah's words, Jesus placed himself in Jeremiah's line and his action in the pattern of the temple sermon: a warning that the temple would fall, which it did in AD 70. The New Testament goes further, presenting Jesus himself as the true temple, the place where God dwells with his people (John 2:19-21), and his people as a temple built of living stones (1 Peter 2:5). The Valley of Hinnom, Ge Hinnom in Hebrew, gave its name to Gehenna, the word Jesus used for final judgment (Matthew 5:22).

hard.q: In verses 22 and 23 does God say he never commanded sacrifices, even though Leviticus is full of them?
hard.a:
The Hebrew of verse 22 can be read as a flat statement that God did not speak to the fathers about burnt offerings and sacrifices when he brought them out of Egypt. Taken alone, that seems to contradict the sacrificial laws of Exodus and Leviticus. Several explanations are offered. Many interpreters see a Hebrew idiom of emphasis, not merely this but that, which is how the BSB renders it (I did not merely command them). On this reading God is setting priorities: his first word at the exodus was obey me (compare Exodus 19:5-6, before the detailed laws of sacrifice), and sacrifice was never meant to stand on its own. Others point out that the Sinai covenant began with the Ten Commandments, not with sacrifice.

Some critical scholars take the verse more literally, as evidence of a prophetic tradition that viewed the sacrificial system as a later development, and they compare Amos 5:25. Most readers across traditions agree on what the verse is doing in context: it is a sharp rebuke to people who thought sacrifice could cover disobedience, in the same spirit as 1 Samuel 15:22 and Hosea 6:6.

questions: What are the modern equivalents of chanting the temple of the LORD, the religious slogans or places people trust instead of God?
Jesus quoted this chapter when he cleared the temple. What would he find if he walked into your church or your own worship today?
God says his first command was obedience, not sacrifice. Where might you be offering God activity in place of obedience?
